item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Archaeology] What did the professor say the sediment cores indicated about rainfall in the settlement's final decades?
choices: That rainfall rose noticeably compared with earlier centuries
That rainfall stayed close to the region's long-term average
That rainfall declined gradually across those decades
That rainfall swung between unusually wet and unusually dry years
item.passage: Transcript: So, Tell Arvani. For a century the story was that the town died of drought — you'll still find that in older textbooks. But the sediment cores tell a different story: through the settlement's final decades, rainfall stayed right around the region's long-term average. Not a slow drying trend, not wild swings from wet to dry, and not some unusual wet period either — ordinary years, one after another. Which removes the easy answer. Now, the storage jars. Everyone assumed grain — big jars, farming town. But the residue analysis came back unambiguous: the large jars had mostly held olive oil, pressed right at the settlement — we have the crushing basins. Not barley from the surrounding fields, not wine hauled in from elsewhere, and no fish residues at all. This was a town producing oil, probably for exchange. What about Kessara, the neighbor? I bring it up for one reason: the team there has been using micro-stratigraphy and full flotation sampling — methods a generation newer than anything used at Arvani — and I want exactly that toolkit brought to our site. To be clear, that is my only point with Kessara: I am not claiming it fell at the same moment, its tablets don't mention Arvani, and whether it carried on afterward is genuinely unsettled. Finally, the earthquake idea. I think it is half right. The tumbled wall sections do look seismic, and the date fits the abandonment — this was no slow decay, and the damage isn't centuries too early. But a town can rebuild walls; this one had rebuilt them before. Shaking may explain some of the damage. It doesn't, by itself, explain why nobody came back.
item.explanation: The professor says that through the final decades rainfall stayed right around the region's long-term average — explicitly not a drying trend, not swings, not a wet period.
item.correct_answer: That rainfall stayed close to the region's long-term average

item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Volcanology] What does the professor say the ground-deformation measurements showed during the unrest episode at the Serrat caldera?
choices: The deformation covered a much smaller area than the first reports claimed
The uplift was centered under the caldera's western rim rather than its middle
The ground rose and then subsided again in a repeating cycle
The uplift went on steadily even after the earthquake swarms had stopped
item.passage: Transcript: Let's talk about the Serrat caldera, two thousand four to twelve. Start with the ground itself. The GPS and the radar agreed: the uplift sat squarely over the center of the caldera, and — this is the part that puzzled everyone — it went on climbing, millimeter by millimeter, long after the earthquake swarms had stopped. There was no sign of the ground settling back, no cycle of rise and fall, and the deformation was every bit as broad as the first reports said. Steady, quiet inflation. Then the gases. The chemistry wouldn't let you call it magma alone, and you couldn't pin it all on heated groundwater either — the emissions carried both signatures at once, magmatic and hydrothermal together, which points to a mixed source: magma degassing into an active water system. And these were not the tired gases of an old, cooling body; the ratios were fresh. Now, why did everyone take this so seriously? Because of the eighteen-sixties. The opening phase of that episode looked strikingly like what the instruments were now recording — the same quiet inflation, the same gas rise — and that episode, remember, ended in an eruption. Observers back then read the signs correctly, as it happens, and its deposits were quarried away long ago, useless for mapping anything. The resemblance was the whole alarm. Which brings us to the alert level. I'll be blunt: when it was raised in oh-eight, the instruments were saying nothing new that week. The newspapers, though, were saying plenty. No one could call the move late, and there was no protocol forcing anyone's hand. The pressure was coming from the public, and the committee moved with it.

item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Art History] What did the professor say the pigment analysis revealed about the blue areas of the Verrine Hours?
choices: The blue is mostly indigo, blended to imitate the look of lapis lazuli
Lapis lazuli was used throughout, even in the minor border decoration
A cheaper azurite base was covered with a thin layer of lapis lazuli
Azurite appears in the margins, while lapis lazuli was reserved for the central figures
item.passage: Transcript: The Verrine Hours. Let's start with what the spectroscopy settled last spring: the blue is lapis, everywhere we looked — the Virgin's robe, yes, but even the little border sprays are lapis. There is no cheaper base layer under it; the lapis goes right down to the parchment, and there is no indigo at all, no azurite anywhere in the book. Now here is my larger point about this workshop, the point I want you to take away: what it used was governed by each patron's purse, not by any rule of the craft. A rich commission, and there is lapis in the margins; a modest one, and the same painters worked wonders with cheap blues. It was never about a house style of materials — and for the record, these compositions match no model book we know, nobody confuses these books with Arden work, and stylistically they kept pace with the newest fashions. It was the money. Which is exactly why I keep returning to the account books: the payments simply stop in the third year, mid-campaign, and that is why the last two gatherings sit unfinished. The accounts never name a single assistant, they don't itemize the pigments, frustratingly, and they won't give you dates precise enough to narrow production — but they do record that break in payment. So: is this Anselm's book? I say yes — but not for the reasons usually given. The faces, if anything, look like assistants' work, and the underdrawing is too varied to be one hand. But the page architecture — the layouts, those border systems — no one else in the region built pages that way, and every page sits comfortably within his working life.
item.explanation: The spectroscopy settled it: the blue is lapis everywhere, even the little border sprays, with no cheaper layers and no substitutes anywhere in the book.

item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Ecology] What did the seedling survey conducted five years after the cyclone show?
choices: Nearly all the new seedlings were clustered along the debris lines the cyclone left

item.passage: Transcript: Marell Atoll, five years after cyclone Osea. The seedling survey came back this spring, and the pattern is odd: nearly everything new is strung along the debris lines — those windrows of wrack the storm left behind. Hardly any seedlings under the parent trees themselves, but along the wrack lines, dense little rows. And to be clear, there was no shortage of seedlings overall, and they were surviving the dry months just fine. Kanari recruitment hasn't collapsed — it has moved. Why? The imperial pigeons disperse the seed, and the follow-up work told us what changed. It isn't the vine — the feeding branches are clear; the vine never reached them. The rats we could rule out too: the exclosures made no difference. And fruiting still lines up with the breeding season the way it always has. No — the flocks are simply too small now. A crop that three hundred birds once cleared in a week hangs there, drops, and rots before the remaining dozens get to it. The storm surge then rakes the fallen fruit into the wrack lines — hence the pattern. Now, people always ask about the mainland kanari forests. I am not pointing to the mainland to say other animals could take over, nor to argue the problem stops at the shoreline, and I am certainly not proposing it as a source of birds. What I am asking is whether anything we learned in those forests transfers to an atoll at all — I doubt the comparison more each year. And yes, we are acting: a small trial, carrying fruit by hand past the surge zone, is already running on the island's two worst-hit stretches. Pigeon counts are still falling, so nobody is waiting on a rebound; we're not opposed to intervening — quite the opposite — and no one has put a translocation of birds on the table.

item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Linguistics] What does the professor say the vocabulary shared by Taruic and Emel indicates about the vowel shift?
choices: The shift was already complete when the words were borrowed
The borrowing ran in the other direction, from Emel into Taruic
The words were borrowed twice, at two different stages of the shift
The shift happened after the borrowing, since Emel preserves the older vowels
item.passage: Transcript: Today, the Taruic vowel shift — and I want to use it to show how much you can squeeze out of very indirect evidence. Start with the vocabulary Taruic shares with its neighbor, Emel. The direction of borrowing isn't in doubt: Taruic into Emel — the cultural terms all run that way. And Emel's borrowed forms keep the old vowels. So the words crossed over before anything had shifted; the shift comes after the borrowing. Each of these words was borrowed once, and once only — there are no doubled forms. Second, how did it spread? It follows the rivers. Every town on the Ossel trade route shifts early; villages a day's walk from the water shift late or not until much later. There is no single center it radiates from. And notice: every word class moved together — this was not a change picking its way through the vocabulary item by item — the records give no hint that careful speech led the way, and wherever it arrived, whole households shifted together, parents along with their children. Third, the 1911 cylinder recordings. The point is not about the era's transcriptions, which are actually rather good. It is this: no speaker on those cylinders mixes the two systems, every village recorded shows the shifted vowels, and the oldest voices, speakers born in the eighteen-thirties, already have the new system entire. The shift was done a century before the cylinders turned. Last, the substrate question — was there an earlier language underneath, pushing this along? We are not guessing in the dark here. The words Taruic took from that earlier language carry precisely these vowels, and the substrate's range, as far as we can trace it, sits exactly where the shift runs deepest. The idea has been argued continuously since the eighteen-nineties — there is nothing to revive — and on the evidence, I would say it stands.

item.prompt: [Academic Talk — History of Science] According to the professor, why did the service's warnings improve in its second decade?
choices: The service began paying fishing crews to report conditions from open water
Telegraph lines finally connected the coastal observation stations
It began pooling its observations with the rival Austrian service
It replaced its old seasonal rules of thumb with warnings based on barometer readings
item.passage: Transcript: The Adriatic storm-warning service. Begin with the wreck of the Stella Maris in December 1873 — two hundred and eleven lives. I tell that story for one reason: it is the event that put the money on the table. Parliament had debated a warning network for years and done nothing; six weeks after the wreck, the funds were voted. Note the order of events — there was no service yet to blame, and no warning had been issued, because none existed to issue. The service's first decade was, honestly, unimpressive. Its second was much better, and here is why: the agreement of 1885. The Adriatic service and its rival, the Austrian network up the coast, began exchanging observations daily by wire. Seeing the rival's pressure field beside your own — that is what sharpened the warnings. The telegraph itself had linked the stations from the very first season, barometers had been the basis of the warnings from day one, and the scheme to pay fishing crews for reports never got past a proposal. It was the pooling that did it. Those barometer ledgers, by the way, survive nearly complete, gathered in one archive in Trieste, and a recalibration team has recently been through the whole series. Their finding: the readings ran consistently low, about two millibars, instrument after instrument. Climate researchers, so far, have shown no interest in the series. And Marini, the founder? A brilliant promoter — the subscriptions, the lecture tours, the medals — but his claims ran well ahead of what his barometers could show. His statistics, it must be said, were ordinary; the organization, frankly, was held together with string; and the public never lost faith in him, not even at the end.
item.explanation: The professor credits the agreement of 1885: the service and the rival Austrian network began exchanging observations daily — it was the pooling that did it.

item.prompt: [Academic Talk — History of Science] What is the professor's judgment of Marini, the service's founder?
choices: A man of ordinary ideas whose real achievement was the organization he built
A reckless forecaster whose premature warnings wore down public trust
A gifted promoter whose scientific claims ran ahead of his evidence
An undervalued figure whose statistical methods anticipated later practice
item.passage: Transcript: The Adriatic storm-warning service. Begin with the wreck of the Stella Maris in December 1873 — two hundred and eleven lives. I tell that story for one reason: it is the event that put the money on the table. Parliament had debated a warning network for years and done nothing; six weeks after the wreck, the funds were voted. Note the order of events — there was no service yet to blame, and no warning had been issued, because none existed to issue. The service's first decade was, honestly, unimpressive. Its second was much better, and here is why: the agreement of 1885. The Adriatic service and its rival, the Austrian network up the coast, began exchanging observations daily by wire. Seeing the rival's pressure field beside your own — that is what sharpened the warnings. The telegraph itself had linked the stations from the very first season, barometers had been the basis of the warnings from day one, and the scheme to pay fishing crews for reports never got past a proposal. It was the pooling that did it. Those barometer ledgers, by the way, survive nearly complete, gathered in one archive in Trieste, and a recalibration team has recently been through the whole series. Their finding: the readings ran consistently low, about two millibars, instrument after instrument. Climate researchers, so far, have shown no interest in the series. And Marini, the founder? A brilliant promoter — the subscriptions, the lecture tours, the medals — but his claims ran well ahead of what his barometers could show. His statistics, it must be said, were ordinary; the organization, frankly, was held together with string; and the public never lost faith in him, not even at the end.
